title: Novel on Kerala’s First Gulf Migrants Wins Yuva Puraskar for Ammar Kizhuparamba
excerpt: ‘Kadal Kandal’ reconstructs the Malabar coast’s perilous pre-oil-boom crossings to the Gulf — the journeys that came before the migration Kerala is known for.
body:
• Malayalam novelist Ammar Kizhuparamba has won the Kerala Sahitya Akademi's Yuva Puraskar 2026 for 'Kadal Kandal', a novel about the first generations of Gulf migrants from Kerala's Malabar coast.
  • The Yuva Puraskar honours writers under 35 and carries ₹50,000 and a copper plaque; the winners were announced in Thrissur on October 13.
  • The novel reconstructs the pre-oil-boom journeys — by dhow and steamer, often without papers — that preceded the Gulf migration Kerala is known for.
  • It is Kizhuparamba's second novel; his first, 'Matsyatar', won the Kairali Books Sargasakthi Award.

The Gulf story Kerala tells about itself usually begins in the 1970s, with the oil boom and the first remittance cheques. Ammar Kizhuparamba's novel 'Kadal Kandal' begins earlier — with the men from the Malabar coast who crossed the Arabian Sea before the boom, in dhows and steamers, chasing work in a Gulf that had no skyscrapers yet. The novel has won the Kerala Sahitya Akademi's Yuva Puraskar for 2026, The Hindu reported.

The award, announced at the Akademi's Changampuzha Hall in Thrissur on October 13, honours writers under 35 and carries a cash prize of ₹50,000 with a copper plaque. It was presented as part of this year's list of Akademi honours for young writers.

The Migration Before the Migration

Kizhuparamba, who is from Kizhuparamba in Malappuram district, built the novel around the undocumented crossings of the pre-boom decades: the agents and brokers who arranged passages, the weeks at sea, the letters that took months to come home, and the households in Malabar that learned to run on money sent from Muscat, Bahrain and the Trucial coast. Malayala Manorama's report on the award described the book as a work of historical reconstruction as much as fiction — an attempt to give names and interior lives to a generation that history mostly recorded as labour.

That generation matters to the Kerala of today. The Gulf Malayali diaspora — now counted in the millions across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and Kuwait — traces its family stories to these crossings. The remittance economy, the Gulf-returned household, even the architecture of Malabar's towns, all begin with men who left before there was a system to leave through.

A Second Novel, a Second Honour

'Kadal Kandal' is Kizhuparamba's second novel. His first, 'Matsyatar', won the Kairali Books Sargasakthi Award, and Malayalam critics have marked him as one of the younger writers working the seam between Malabar's history and its present. The Yuva Puraskar is meant to spot exactly that kind of writer early, and at under 35, Kizhuparamba has time on his side.

Malayalam literature has been here before: Benyamin's 'Aadujeevitham' (Goat Days) made the Gulf migrant's ordeal a modern classic and, later, a major film. Where Benyamin wrote the boom years' brutality, Kizhuparamba reaches back to the crossings that made the boom possible — the generation whose sacrifices rarely made it into print at all.

For readers in the Gulf diaspora, the timing has a neat symmetry: a novel about the grandfathers of Gulf migration, honoured in the week Kerala's extended family — at home and in the Gulf — prepares for Diwali. The first copies those grandparents' grandchildren buy may well be in Dubai and Doha.
